description: Hi everyone! I'm a B.Tech CSE–Data Science student interested in astronomy, space exploration, and machine learning. I'm familiar with Python and eager to work on data analysis and visualization. Looking to join a supportive team to build something amazing!
summary:
We built an interactive web platform featuring a cinematic flyover of the 2025 SPHEREx all-sky map, dynamic wavelength comparison sliders, a 102-band spectral breakdown (0.75–5.0 μm), and a curated catalog of celestial targets—from solar system planets to distant spiral galaxies.

How It Addresses the Challenge:
Raw multi-spectral data can overwhelm non-specialists. By pairing official NASA/JPL-Caltech visualizations and NASA/IPAC IRSA resources with hands-on visual tools, our platform lets users interactively compare infrared color maps and explore cosmic phenomena step by step without needing technical expertise.

Why It Is Important:
Infrared light pierces cosmic dust to reveal cooler objects and the early history of galaxies hidden from visible-light telescopes. SPHEREx Cosmic Explorer bridges cutting-edge NASA mission science with public curiosity, empowering students and enthusiasts to explore how the universe evolved.
details:
1. Comprehensive Project Description (For NASA Space Apps Submission Form)

Bridging the Gap Between Infrared Spectroscopy and Public Exploration

NASA’s Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ice Explorer (SPHEREx) captures the entire sky across 102 near-infrared spectral channels spanning 0.75 to 5.0 micrometers. While this dataset offers unprecedented insight into cosmic inflation, galaxy evolution, and biogenic ices, multi-band spectroscopic data presents a steep barrier to entry for students, educators, and the general public. Without specialized astronomical software or domain expertise, raw spectral cubes and technical archive catalogs remain largely inaccessible outside the research community.

SPHEREx Cosmic Explorer addresses this accessibility gap by translating the mission’s scientific framework and all-sky infrared observations into an intuitive, browser-based educational environment. Designed as a public-facing gateway to infrared astrophysics, the application combines official mission products with interactive comparison tools and structured navigation to help users understand how SPHEREx observes the cosmos and what infrared wavelengths reveal.

Key Capabilities & Implemented Architecture

  • Interactive All-Sky Visual Comparison: Built around NASA/JPL-Caltech’s reduced-resolution all-sky infrared mosaic (compiled from observations collected between May and December 2025), the platform features an interactive split-screen slider that contrasts the SPHEREx infrared color map against a color-suppressed view. This visual transformation demonstrates how mapping 102 infrared bands into visible colors isolates stars, hot gas, and cosmic dust that would otherwise appear indistinct.
  • Structured Mission & Spectrum Pathways: Rather than overwhelming users with raw FITS files, the interface organizes exploration into dedicated modules—Explore, Science, Mission, and Spectrum—guiding learners sequentially from photon collection across six detector/filter assemblies to cosmological investigation.
  • Curated Astronomical Object Catalog: Users can browse a curated catalog of 16 distinct celestial targets—ranging from Solar System planets (Mercury through Neptune) and nearby stellar nurseries (Orion Nebula, Pleiades) to deep-sky structures (Andromeda Galaxy, Sombrero Galaxy, Crab Nebula, and the Cosmic Web)—complete with right ascension/declination coordinates and dedicated object profiles.
  • Transparent Data Provenance: To maintain scientific integrity, the platform explicitly distinguishes between official NASA/JPL-Caltech all-sky map products, illustrative visual transforms, and curated educational object records, ensuring users understand the exact scope and origin of the data they are exploring.

Educational Impact & Honest Scope

SPHEREx Cosmic Explorer is engineered for immediate zero-install accessibility across modern web browsers, serving as a visual teaching aid for classrooms and self-directed learners. Currently, the application functions as an educational visualization and catalog explorer rather than a live FITS data-processing pipeline or coordinate-accurate sky-overlay engine—the curated object profiles represent standalone astronomical references rather than live positional overlays on the static all-sky mosaic.

By pairing authentic NASA/JPL-Caltech imagery with clear spectroscopic storytelling, the project lays a scalable foundation for future integration with NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) APIs, demonstrating how thoughtful interface design can turn complex space-mission data into an engaging public resource.

2. Short Version (For Word/Character-Limited Fields)

SPHEREx Cosmic Explorer is an interactive, browser-based astronomy web application built to make NASA’s SPHEREx mission and near-infrared spectroscopy accessible to students and the public. Because 102-channel infrared datasets (0.75–5.0 μm) typically require specialized software to interpret, the platform translates SPHEREx’s core science into an intuitive visual experience.

Featuring an interactive split-screen slider comparing NASA/JPL-Caltech’s all-sky infrared mosaic against a color-suppressed view, the app visually demonstrates how infrared wavelengths uncover cosmic dust, cooler stars, and distant galaxies hidden in plain sight. Users can explore dedicatedMission and Spectrum modules alongside a curated 16-object catalog—complete with RA/Dec coordinates and scientific profiles—while clear provenance labels distinguish official NASA imagery from educational catalog entries. SPHEREx Cosmic Explorer lowers the barrier to infrared astrophysics and establishes a modular foundation for future archive integration.

3. Standout Innovative Aspects for Judges

  • Pedagogical "Split-View" Visual Comparison: Instead of simply displaying a static press-release image, the interactive drag-slider between the SPHEREx color-mapped mosaic and its color-suppressed counterpart gives users hands-on intuition for why multi-channel infrared mapping isolates physical phenomena (dust vs. hot gas vs. stars).
  • Scientific Rigor & Provenance Transparency: Student projects often blur the line between real mission data and mockups. This application explicitly notes on-screen when an image is an illustrative transform versus an official NASA/JPL-Caltech product and clearly clarifies that the curated object catalog is a separate educational dataset rather than live plotted coordinates on the mosaic.
  • Progressive Information Architecture: The user journey mirrors the scientific method—moving cleanly from Observe (light collection) and Measure (0.75–5.0 μm spectral separation) to Map and Investigate, making instrumentation concepts (such as the six detector/filter assemblies) digestible without oversimplifying the physics.
  • Zero-Friction Public Accessibility: Hosted as a lightweight, responsive web application requiring no downloads, accounts, or specialized astronomical tools, making it immediately usable in high school and undergraduate STEM outreach.

4. How the Project Addresses the SPHEREx Challenge

The core challenge of SPHEREx lies in communicating the value of all-sky imaging spectroscopy—specifically, how capturing 102 distinct infrared color bands across the entire sky unlocks scientific questions that traditional single-band optical telescopes cannot answer.

SPHEREx Cosmic Explorer directly addresses this challenge by:

  1. Demystifying Wavelengths: Giving users a direct visual mechanism to compare infrared color mapping against suppressed views, illustrating how spectral separation reveals obscured cosmic structures.
  2. Connecting Instrumentation to Discovery: Linking SPHEREx’s hardware capabilities (0.75–5.0 μm range, 102 spectral bands, 2025 all-sky survey mosaic) directly to tangible astronomical targets in the curated catalog.
  3. Lowering Technical Barriers: Providing a clean, structured web interface that bridges the gap between raw public archives (NASA/IPAC IRSA) and everyday learners curious about the infrared universe.
